Here’s something I learned early in this job. An ad is never just information. Somebody paid to print it, and they wanted something from you. Your money, your help, or you, on a ship. So read these two ads like a skeptic. Ask yourself: who made this, and what do they want me to do?

Here’s a trick I use when a story sounds too simple. Try it yourself. The Herald says New Englanders built their towns the way they liked. So you build one. Pick something, put it on the land, and listen to what the land says back. Then decide: was it all just what people liked?

A chain is only as strong as its links, so read each one before you place it. Some links are about the land. Some are about what people believed. And the last few are about people who didn’t get a say at all. Take those slowly. Watch for the one link that really was a choice.

This page is set like a real newspaper, in columns. Six people, one day. When you move the sun, read across, not just down. Compare the planter and the enslaved person at the same hour. They lived on the same land, but their days were nothing alike. And watch the button that moves the sun. The Herald will try to sneak in a claim. Don’t print it until you check it.
